title: Project management
summary: Contract types and the Public Procurement Act 2063 are the examinable core, and the item-rate contract dominates civil work because quantities cannot be fixed in advance — which means the EMPLOYER carries the quantity risk. Understand why cost-plus-percentage has a perverse incentive, and know liquidated damages as a pre-agreed genuine pre-estimate of loss rather than a penalty. For quality, keep QA (process-oriented, preventive) apart from QC (product-oriented, detective), and remember Pareto: 80 percent of problems come from 20 percent of causes.

sections.heading: Project management framework
sections.body:
**The triple constraint** — the three that trade against one another, with **quality** at the centre:

> **SCOPE · TIME · COST**, and **QUALITY** as the outcome

**Change any one and at least one other must move.** Promising all three fixed — the full scope, by the original date, within the original budget — is the root of most project failure, because something then gives silently, and it is usually **quality** or **safety**.

**Knowledge areas (PMBOK):**

| Area | Concerns |
|---|---|
| **Integration** | Coordinating everything else; **change control** |
| **Scope** | What is and is not included; the **WBS** |
| **Schedule** | Activities, sequence, durations, control |
| **Cost** | Estimating, budgeting, control |
| **Quality** | Planning, assurance, control |
| **Resource** | Team and physical resources |
| **Communications** | Information to stakeholders |
| **Risk** | Identification, analysis, response, monitoring |
| **Procurement** | Contracts and suppliers |
| **Stakeholder** | Identification and engagement |

**Process groups:** **Initiating → Planning → Executing → Monitoring and Controlling → Closing** — with monitoring running throughout rather than after.

**Organisation structures**, and the trade-off is worth knowing:

| Structure | Authority of the project manager | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Functional** | **Low** — the functional heads hold authority | Specialists grouped by discipline; good technical depth, **poor project focus** |
| **Weak matrix** | Limited | — |
| **Balanced matrix** | Shared | — |
| **Strong matrix** | High | — |
| **Projectised** | **HIGHEST** — full authority over a dedicated team | Excellent project focus; **duplication of resources** between projects, and staff have no home when it ends |

**The matrix exists to resolve the conflict** between the functional structure's technical depth and the projectised structure's focus — at the cost of every team member having **two bosses**, which is its characteristic difficulty and a common source of dysfunction.

**Risk management**, in sequence:

> **Identify → Analyse (qualitative, then quantitative) → Plan responses → Implement → Monitor**

**Qualitative analysis** scores each risk by **probability × impact** and ranks them on a **risk matrix**. **Quantitative analysis** uses **expected monetary value**, **decision trees**, **sensitivity analysis** and **Monte Carlo simulation**.

**Risk responses**, for **threats** and for **opportunities**:

| Threat response | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **AVOID** | Change the plan so the risk cannot occur |
| **TRANSFER** | Shift the consequence to another party — **insurance, a fixed-price contract, a bond, a warranty** |
| **MITIGATE** | Reduce the probability or the impact |
| **ACCEPT** | Take it knowingly, with a **contingency** if active |

**Transfer does not eliminate the risk** — it moves who bears it, and the other party **prices it**. A fixed-price contract transfers cost risk to the contractor, who adds a premium for it; if the risk is one the contractor cannot control or assess, that premium is large and the employer pays for uncertainty rather than for work. **The efficient allocation is to give each risk to the party best able to CONTROL it** — which is the principle underlying every sensible contract form, and the reason ground risk is usually retained by the employer while workmanship risk sits with the contractor.

**Contingency and reserve:**

| Type | For | Controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| **Contingency reserve** | **KNOWN unknowns** — identified risks | The **project manager** |
| **Management reserve** | **UNKNOWN unknowns** | **Senior management** |

**Stakeholders** in a civil project: the **client/employer**, the **contractor and subcontractors**, the **consultant/engineer**, **funders**, **regulatory authorities**, the **affected community**, **land owners**, **users**, and **suppliers**. Identifying them and managing their expectations is a project activity in its own right, and the **affected community** is the one most often neglected — and the one most capable of stopping a project.

sections.heading: Contracts and tendering
sections.body:
**Types of contract**, and the discriminator is **who carries which risk**:

| Type | Payment basis | **Quantity risk** | Suits |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ITEM RATE (unit price)** | **Measured quantity × tendered rate** | **EMPLOYER** | **MOST CIVIL WORKS** — quantities cannot be fixed in advance |
| **LUMP SUM** | One **fixed price** for the defined work | **CONTRACTOR** | Well-defined work with **complete drawings** |
| **Percentage rate** | A **percentage above or below** the employer's estimate | Employer | Where the estimate is reliable |
| **Cost plus percentage** | Actual cost **+ an agreed %** | **Employer entirely** | **Emergency** work; scope unknown |
| **Cost plus fixed fee** | Actual cost **+ a fixed sum** | Employer, but the fee is capped | Better incentive than the above |
| **Target cost** | Cost plus a fee, with a **shared saving or overrun** | Shared | Collaborative working |
| Labour rate | Labour only; the employer supplies material | Employer | Departmental work |
| **Design and build (turnkey)** | One party designs and constructs | Contractor | Where a single point of responsibility is wanted |
| **EPC** | Engineering, procurement, construction | Contractor | Plant and industrial projects |
| **BOT / BOOT** | Build, own, operate, transfer | Concessionaire | Infrastructure with a revenue stream |

**Why the ITEM RATE contract dominates civil works** — the reasoning is worth stating:

> Quantities in construction can rarely be fixed exactly in advance. **Excavation depths, foundation levels and ground conditions all vary from the drawings.** An item rate contract prices each **item** and pays for the **quantity actually executed**, so neither party has to gamble on the quantity.

The employer therefore carries the **quantity** risk (paying for what is actually built) while the contractor carries the **rate** risk (having priced each item). That allocation matches the principle above: the employer, who commissioned the site investigation and owns the ground, is better placed to bear ground quantity risk than a contractor who saw the site for a day.

**The perverse incentive in COST PLUS PERCENTAGE:**

> The contractor's **fee RISES with the cost**, so there is **no incentive whatever to economise** — and an active incentive to inflate.

It is therefore used **only where the scope genuinely cannot be defined** — emergency work, urgent repairs, investigation-led work — and a **fixed fee** version is preferred wherever possible, because the fee then no longer grows with the spend. Many public procurement rules restrict or prohibit the percentage form for exactly this reason.

**Tendering — the process:**

> **Notice → Sale/issue of documents → Pre-bid meeting → Submission → Opening → Evaluation → Award → Agreement**

**Methods under Nepal's Public Procurement Act 2063 (2007)** and Regulations 2064:

| Method | Applies |
|---|---|
| **Open competitive bidding** — **National (NCB)** or **International (ICB)** | Above the prescribed threshold; the default |
| **Sealed quotation** | Smaller value |
| **Direct procurement** | Very small value, or a single-source justification |
| **Force account** (departmental execution) | Where the agency does the work itself |
| **Framework agreement** | Repeated small purchases |
| Limited/restricted tendering | Specialised work, prequalified bidders |

**The thresholds determine which method may be used**, and using a lower-competition method above its threshold is a procurement irregularity, not a matter of convenience.

**Tender documents** comprise: the **notice**, **instructions to bidders**, **conditions of contract (general and particular)**, **specifications**, **drawings**, **bill of quantities**, **forms of bid and agreement**, and the **schedules**.

**Securities and financial instruments (Nepal PPA 2063):**

| Instrument | Amount | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **Bid security (earnest money)** | **2 – 3%** of the estimated cost | Guarantees the bid is not **withdrawn** and that the winner signs |
| **Performance security** | **5 – 10%** of the contract price | Guarantees **performance** of the contract |
| **Retention money** | Typically **5%**, withheld from each bill | Guarantees rectification of **defects**; released after the **defect liability period** |
| **Mobilisation advance** | Up to a stated percentage, **against a bank guarantee** | Enables the contractor to start |
| Advance payment guarantee | Equal to the advance | Secures its recovery |

**Evaluation** is on the basis stated in the documents — usually the **lowest evaluated substantially responsive bid**, after checking **responsiveness**, **arithmetic**, and **qualification**. **An abnormally low bid is a risk, not a bargain**: it commonly ends in claims, poor quality, or abandonment, and most procurement rules allow it to be investigated and, if unjustified, rejected.

**Contract administration during execution:**

| Instrument | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Variation order** | Instructs a **change**; valued at **contract rates** where the work is of the same character, otherwise at negotiated rates |
| **Interim (running) bill** | Payment for work done to date, on measurement |
| **Extension of time (EOT)** | Extends the completion date for **excusable** delay |
| **Liquidated damages** | Deduction for **culpable** delay |
| **Price adjustment (escalation)** | Where provided, for material and labour price changes |
| **Defect liability certificate** | On satisfactory completion of the defects period |
| **Final bill and completion certificate** | Closure |

**Variation orders must be issued IN WRITING and IN ADVANCE**, and there are **two reasons**, of which the second is often forgotten:

1. It authorises the **payment** for the additional work.
2. It provides the documentary basis for an **EXTENSION OF TIME** — without it, the contractor is exposed to **liquidated damages for a delay the employer caused**.

**Liquidated damages:**

> A **PRE-AGREED sum deducted for each day or week of delay** in completion, fixed **in the contract itself** before any delay occurs — commonly a small percentage per week, subject to an overall **ceiling of about 10%**.

**Why pre-agreed rather than proved:**

| Advantage | For whom |
|---|---|
| No need to **prove** actual loss | Employer |
| **Certainty** of the maximum exposure | Contractor |
| Avoids litigation over the amount | Both |

**The legal requirement that governs them:**

> Liquidated damages must be a **GENUINE PRE-ESTIMATE of the likely loss**, **NOT a punishment**. A sum set extravagantly above any conceivable loss is a **PENALTY**, and a penalty is generally **unenforceable**.

That distinction — **liquidated damages versus penalty** — is the central legal point of the topic and is examined directly.

**Extension of time** is the contractor's defence, and LD can only be levied for delay that is the **contractor's responsibility**. Grounds for an EOT:

| Ground | Example |
|---|---|
| **Employer's delay** | Late possession of site, late drawings, late decisions or approvals |
| **Variations** | Additional work instructed |
| **Force majeure** | Earthquake, flood, strike, epidemic, war |
| **Exceptionally adverse weather** | Beyond what was reasonably foreseeable |
| **Suspension** ordered by the employer | — |
| Delay by other contractors employed by the employer | — |

**Concurrent delay** — where employer-caused and contractor-caused delay overlap — is the hard case, and practice varies: some contracts grant time but not money, which is the usual compromise.

**Dispute resolution**, in escalating order:

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Negotiation** | Direct; cheapest and fastest |
| **Mediation / conciliation** | A neutral facilitates a settlement; **non-binding** |
| **Adjudication / Dispute Board** | A rapid, provisionally **binding** decision during the works |
| **Arbitration** | A binding award; **private**, and enforceable |
| **Litigation** | The courts; slow, public, expensive |

**Arbitration is the usual contractual mechanism** in construction, and its advantages are **speed, privacy, and a tribunal with technical expertise**. Its disadvantages are cost and limited grounds of appeal. **Dispute Boards** — a standing panel visiting the site — have gained ground because they resolve issues **while the works proceed**, rather than accumulating them for a battle at the end. Nepal's **Arbitration Act 2055 (1999)** governs arbitration.

sections.heading: Quality management
sections.body:
**Quality is CONFORMANCE TO REQUIREMENTS — fitness for purpose.** It is not "the best possible", which is **grade**, a different concept: a low-grade product of high quality (a simple item that does exactly what it should) is entirely acceptable, while a high-grade product of low quality is not.

**The three processes, and the QA/QC distinction is examined every time:**

| Process | Orientation | Character | Asks |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Quality PLANNING** | — | Determines the standards and how to meet them | *What is required?* |
| **Quality ASSURANCE (QA)** | **PROCESS**-oriented | **PREVENTIVE** — audits and improves the **process** | *Are we doing the right things, the right way?* |
| **Quality CONTROL (QC)** | **PRODUCT**-oriented | **DETECTIVE** — inspects and tests the **product** | *Did this item meet the specification?* |

> **QA is process-oriented and preventive; QC is product-oriented and detective.**

A concrete example makes it concrete: **QC** is testing the cube at 28 days; **QA** is the system of approved mix designs, calibrated batching plant, trained operators and documented curing that makes the cube likely to pass. QC finds the failure; QA prevents it.

**Cost of quality**, and the ratio between the categories is the argument:

| Category | Cost |
|---|---|
| **Prevention** | Training, planning, process design, calibration |
| **Appraisal** | Inspection, testing, audit |
| **Internal failure** | Rework, scrap, re-testing — found **before** handover |
| **External failure** | Warranty claims, repairs, damage to reputation, **liability** — found **after** |

> **Prevention is far cheaper than appraisal, which is far cheaper than failure — and internal failure is far cheaper than external.**

The conventional rule of thumb is a factor of ten at each step. That is the entire economic case for QA, and it is why a project that "cannot afford" a quality system invariably spends more on rework than the system would have cost.

**The seven basic quality tools (Ishikawa):**

| Tool | Use |
|---|---|
| **Check sheet** | Systematic data collection |
| **Histogram** | The **distribution** of a variable |
| **PARETO chart** | Ranks causes by frequency or cost |
| **Cause-and-effect (Ishikawa / FISHBONE) diagram** | Explores the possible **causes** of one effect |
| **Scatter diagram** | Relationship between two variables |
| **CONTROL chart** | Distinguishes **normal variation** from an **assignable cause** |
| **Stratification / flow chart** | Separating data by source; mapping the process |

**The Pareto principle:**

> **About 80% of the problems arise from about 20% of the causes.**

So effort should be directed at the **vital few** rather than spread over the **trivial many** — which is the single most useful management heuristic in the subchapter, and applies as much to defects and delays as to costs.

**The control chart** deserves explanation because it embodies a genuine statistical idea: every process varies, and the chart distinguishes **common cause variation** (inherent, random, requiring a change to the **process** to reduce) from **special (assignable) cause variation** (an identifiable event, requiring **investigation of that instance**). Reacting to common-cause variation as though it were special — "tampering" — actually **increases** the variation, which is counter-intuitive and well established.

**Quality systems and standards:**

| System | Character |
|---|---|
| **ISO 9000 series** | Quality **management system** standard; certification of the **system**, not the product |
| **Total Quality Management (TQM)** | Organisation-wide, **continuous improvement**, customer focus, employee involvement |
| **Six Sigma** | Statistical, defect-reduction focused (**DMAIC**) |
| **Kaizen** | Continuous incremental improvement |
| **PDCA (Deming) cycle** | **Plan – Do – Check – Act**, iterated |

**ISO 9001 certifies the SYSTEM, not the product** — a widely misunderstood point. A certified organisation has documented processes and follows them; it does not follow that its output is of any particular quality standard, only that it is **consistent** and **traceable**.

**Quality control in civil construction** — the practical content:

| Item | Control |
|---|---|
| **Materials** | Testing on receipt against the specification; **approved sources**; certificates |
| **Concrete** | Mix design, **cube tests**, slump, batching accuracy, **curing records** |
| **Reinforcement** | Grade, size, **cover**, spacing, laps — checked **before concreting** |
| **Earthwork** | **Field density** tests, moisture content, layer thickness |
| **Bituminous work** | Binder content, gradation, **Marshall stability**, laid **density (cores)**, temperature |
| **Workmanship** | Line, level, plumb, finish, tolerances |
| **Records** | **Test certificates, pour cards, inspection reports, as-built drawings** |

**Checking reinforcement BEFORE concreting is the classic hold point**, and the reason is obvious once stated: once the concrete is placed, the reinforcement cannot be inspected, corrected or even seen. The same logic applies to **buried services, waterproofing, and any work that will be covered** — which is why a construction quality plan defines **hold points** at which work may not proceed without inspection, and **witness points** at which the engineer may attend.

**Inspection and Test Plan (ITP)** is the document that sets those out: for each activity, **what is checked, by whom, against what standard, at what frequency, and what record is produced** — and whether it is a hold point, a witness point or a surveillance point.

**Non-conformance and its handling:**

> **Identify → Record (non-conformance report) → Evaluate → Decide: REWORK, REPAIR, ACCEPT (by concession, with justification), or REJECT → Verify → Analyse the CAUSE → Corrective action to prevent recurrence**

**The last step is what separates a quality system from an inspection regime.** Rectifying a defect fixes one instance; **identifying and removing its cause** prevents the next hundred. A project that repeatedly rectifies the same defect has an inspection system and no quality system.

**Acceptance of non-conforming work by concession** deserves a professional note: it is legitimate where a **documented engineering assessment** shows the work still meets its performance requirements — and illegitimate as an informal accommodation. The assessment must be **explicit, justified and signed**, because it is a decision to depart from the specification and someone must own it.

sections.heading: Construction safety and site management
sections.body:
**Construction is among the most hazardous industries**, and in Nepal the position is worse than the statistics suggest, because much work is informal and unrecorded.

**The principal hazards and their controls:**

| Hazard | Typical cause | Control |
|---|---|---|
| **FALLS FROM HEIGHT** | Scaffolding, edges, openings, roofs, ladders | **Guard rails, toe boards, full boarding, harnesses, edge protection, covers over openings** |
| **Excavation collapse** | Unsupported trench, spoil at the edge, water | **Timbering/shoring, battering, spoil set back, dewatering, safe access** |
| **Struck by falling material** | Loads, tools, debris | Helmets, **toe boards and netting**, exclusion zones, no throwing |
| **Struck by plant** | Reversing, slewing, blind spots | **Segregation of plant and people**, banksmen, reversing alarms |
| **Electrocution** | Overhead lines, damaged cables, temporary supply | Isolation, **permits**, RCDs, clearance from overhead lines |
| **Collapse of temporary works** | Formwork, falsework, scaffolding | **DESIGN of temporary works**, competent erection, inspection |
| **Confined space** | Manholes, tanks, sewers, deep excavations | **Gas testing, ventilation, permit-to-work, harness and attendant** |
| Lifting operations | Overload, poor slinging, ground failure | Lift plan, competent slinger and operator, certified gear |
| Fire | Hot work, fuel, waste | Permits, extinguishers, housekeeping |
| Health | Dust (silica), noise, vibration, chemicals, manual handling | Extraction, PPE, rotation, health surveillance |

**Falls from height are the leading cause of construction fatality**, which is why **scaffolding, edge protection and openings** deserve disproportionate attention. A scaffold is a **temporary structure that must nevertheless be DESIGNED**, erected by competent people, and **inspected before first use, after alteration and after bad weather** — and it is precisely because it is temporary that it is treated casually and fails.

**The hierarchy of control** — and the order is the point, not the list:

| Rank | Control | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. ELIMINATE** | Remove the hazard entirely | **Design out** the need to work at height — prefabricate at ground level |
| **2. SUBSTITUTE** | Replace with something less hazardous | A less toxic solvent; a smaller unit that needs no crane |
| **3. ENGINEERING controls** | Isolate people from the hazard | **Guard rails, edge protection, machine guards, ventilation** |
| **4. ADMINISTRATIVE controls** | Change the way people work | Permits, training, signage, rotation, method statements |
| **5. PPE** | Protect the individual | Helmet, harness, boots, goggles, respirator |

> **PPE is the LAST resort, not the first** — because it protects **only the wearer**, only if **worn correctly**, and it **fails silently**. Every level above it protects everyone present, regardless of their behaviour.

A site whose safety programme consists of issuing helmets has not begun. **Designing out the hazard is the most effective measure and the cheapest**, because it is done on paper — which is the argument for **design for safety** (or **prevention through design**): the designer's decisions determine much of the risk the constructor will face, and the designer is the only person who can eliminate it.

**Safety management elements:**

| Element | Content |
|---|---|
| **Safety policy** | Signed commitment, responsibilities |
| **Risk assessment and method statement (RAMS)** | Per activity, before it starts |
| **Induction and training** | Every person on site; toolbox talks |
| **Permit-to-work** | For **confined space, hot work, excavation, live electrical, lifting** |
| **Inspection regime** | Scaffolds, excavations, plant, lifting gear |
| **Incident reporting and investigation** | Including **near misses** |
| **Emergency plan** | First aid, evacuation, rescue, contacts |
| Welfare | Water, sanitation, rest, accommodation |

**Reporting NEAR MISSES is the most valuable and most neglected practice**, and the reasoning is statistical: for every serious injury there are many minor ones and a great many near misses arising from the **same underlying causes**. Investigating near misses therefore addresses those causes at **no human cost** — whereas waiting for the injury means learning the same lesson at the highest possible price.

**Legal framework in Nepal:** the **Labour Act 2074 (2017)** and Labour Rules place duties on the employer for a safe workplace, and the **Public Procurement Act** and standard contract documents impose safety obligations on the contractor. Enforcement is weaker than the law, which places a correspondingly greater burden on the **professional judgement of the engineer** — who is often the only person on site with both the knowledge to recognise a hazard and the authority to stop the work.

**Site organisation and layout** — a genuine planning task, not an afterthought:

| Consideration | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Access and haul routes** | Separate **plant and pedestrian** routes; adequate turning; wheel washing |
| **Material storage** | Near the point of use; **cement dry and off the ground**; aggregate on a hard base, separated by type; reinforcement off the ground |
| **Plant location** | Batching plant, crane, workshop — sited to minimise double handling |
| **Site offices and welfare** | Water, sanitation, first aid, rest area, **accommodation** where the site is remote |
| **Security and hoarding** | Public protection, theft |
| **Utilities** | Power, water, drainage, communications |
| **Waste and spoil** | Segregation, designated tips |
| **Drainage** | Site kept drained — a flooded site is unsafe and unproductive |

**Minimising double handling** is the organising principle of site layout: every time material is moved twice, the cost is paid twice and the opportunity for damage and injury doubles. Storing cement three hundred metres from the mixer is a small planning failure that is paid for on every bag.

**Construction equipment selection:**

| Factor | Consideration |
|---|---|
| **Quantity and rate of work** | Determines the size and number of machines |
| **Site conditions** | Access, ground bearing, space, gradient |
| **Availability of spares and skilled operators** | **Decisive in a remote location** |
| **Owning versus hiring** | Hire for short duration and specialised plant; own for continuous use |
| Fuel and power availability | — |
| Balance of the fleet | Excavator, hauler and compactor outputs must **match** |

**Balancing the fleet is the point most often missed**: an excavator loading trucks at 100 m³/hour, served by trucks that can only remove 60 m³/hour, is an excavator idle 40% of the time. The output of the whole operation is that of its **slowest element**, so matching the components is worth more than upgrading any one of them.

**Owning or hiring** deserves the closing note, because it is the question a contractor actually faces. **Owning** suits plant with **high, continuous utilisation** and justifies the capital, maintenance organisation and operator training; **hiring** suits **short-duration, specialised or peak-demand** plant and converts a fixed cost into a variable one. The **break-even utilisation** — typically around **50 to 60%** — is computed by comparing the **EUAC of ownership** against the hire rate, which is exactly the engineering economy calculation of the previous subchapter applied to a real decision.
